newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Troops called in after violent Albanian protests.
newsitem.headline: Troops called in after violent Albanian protests.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha, facing his biggest crisis since winning power in 1992, turned to the army to restore order after protesters clashed with riot police in the capital and wreaked destruction in the south.

Rage over collapsing savings schemes in which Albanians have poured millions of dollars turned to violence as demonstrators around the Balkan state stoned police and set fire to government buildings in mounting protests against the ruling right-wing Democrats.
Armed troops were already on alert in Tirana late on Sunday, guarding ministries, the central bank and other strategic points.

The Interior Ministry said around 84 police officers were injured, some seriously, in the weekend clashes. About 30 people were arrested, but there were no official figures for the number of protesters hurt.
A fresh demonstration was scheduled for Monday in the northern city of Shkoder where authorities called for a peaceful protest.
"Considering the events of the past few days...we urge the population of Shkoder to distance itself from violent acts," the city council said in a statement.

Albania's parliament, sitting for the first time on a Sunday since the Democrats swept to power in a 1992 general election, voted at an emergency session to give Berisha the power to deploy troops to unblock roads and guard government buildings.

"This decision has nothing to do with a state of emergency but the traffic, water depots, oil reserves, town halls...and strategic sites should not be attacked," Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu told Reuters after the meeting.
Shehu was beaten about the head by demonstrators and forced to take refuge in a soccer stadium when he visited the southern town of Lushnje on Saturday to try to calm a protest there.
Protests have escalated across the former hardline communist state after some pyramid savings schemes began to collapse, leaving many impoverished Albanians facing destitution.
Thousands of people sold homes and livestock, or used cash sent from relatives working abroad, to invest in schemes promising returns of around 200 percent in three months.

Businesses and shops, even food retailers, reported a plunge in earnings as people stopped spending to invest. Some estimates put the total amount of money involved at hundreds of millions of dollars -- a huge sum in Europe's poorest nation.

The tensions erupted into violence when thousands of people, accompanied by opposition party leaders, converged on central Tirana on Sunday and clashed with riot police, who used batons and water cannon to disperse them.
Albanian television showed aerial pictures of disturbances in more than a dozen other cities or towns where protesters set fire to town halls, courts and offices of the ruling Democrats.
The violence was the most serious in Albania since 1991, when about 40 people were killed in food riots.
State television broadcast pictures showing smoke billowing out of the burnt-out headquarters of the local Democratic Party in the southeastern town of Korca near the border with Greece.

In Berat, 120 km (75 miles) south of Tirana, protesters set fire to the court and offices of the state prosecutor. Government and Democratic Party buildings were also burnt in the southwestern towns of Fier and Vlore.
In an effort to appease enraged investors, Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi assured them they would get their money back with interest from February 5.

Authorities have seized around $300 million in two pyramid scheme accounts but it was unlikely to be enough. The government, already burdened by a big budget deficit, has little other cash at its disposal.
